title: multi-tenant-cpu-priority-probe-notes
body:
Context:
This is an exploratory scratchpad for CPU-side tail and throughput issues we see on multi-tenant hosts. Multiple tenants with mixed request sizes are showing increased p99 for small requests under medium-high CPU load (~65-85%). High-level symptom: short-chat style requests (<= 80 tokens input) occasionally spike to 2-4x expected latency while long requests remain largely unaffected. Hypothesis space includes: tokenizer cost variability, JSON/header parsing, frequent parking/unparking of short work units, Python GIL and interpreter overhead for tiny handler paths, and syscalls caused by our threadpool coordination.

Goal:
- Identify dominant CPU hotspots for small requests under contention.
- Propose low-risk mitigations that improve small-request p95/p99 without regressing long-request throughput.
- Produce an A/B plan for rollout and instrumentation.

Environment + instrumentation used:
- Machines: c5a.4x (16 vCPU) emulator nodes for unit testing; test cluster uses g5.2x + 64GB mem for representative workloads.
- Workload generator: custom harness (tools/loadgen-mt), mixed tenant profiles (70% small, 30% large), poisson arrivals, configurable QPS.
- Profiling: perf (cycles, cache-misses), bpftrace scripts for wakeups/context-switches, py-spy sampling (30Hz), eBPF uprobe hooks for our Rust tokenizer and C++ infer shim, strace for syscall distribution on a subset.
- Metrics captured: p50/p95/p99 latency per-size band, CPU tokens/s, syscall rate (futex/eventfd/read/write), ctx-switches/s, wakeups/s, GIL hold-time (py-spy derived), time-in-tokenizer (in ns) from uprobe.

Summary of quick experiments (short-form):
1) Baseline mixed workload (70% small requests): p99 small = 210ms, p95 small = 90ms, CPU util ~72%. Tokenizer uprobe time accounted for ~28% of CPU samples on small requests. JSON header parse ~12%. Python handler (before handing to Rust/C++) ~18%. Rest is scheduler/futex/wakeup (~18%) and syscalls ~6%.
2) Run with SIMD-enabled tokenizer extension: p95 small dropped 30% (from 90ms -> 62ms), p99 small dropped 22% (210ms -> 164ms). Tokenizer CPU share reduced to 15%. However observed higher branch-mispredict events on < 40B inputs causing small increase in variance for micro-bursts.
3) Single-threaded request-affinity test (bind small-request workers to specific cores, reduce cross-core wakeups): p99 small 160ms, ctx-switches/s down 42%, but throughput for long requests decreased 8% due to less global scheduling flexibility.
4) Switch threadpool to eventfd-based park/unpark (replacing futex path) in prototype: measured syscalls/s decreased 25%, wakeups/s down 30%, p99 small improved to 150ms. But CPU burn for idle threads slightly higher (spin fallback).
5) Move header parsing to a tiny Rust pre-parse (zero-GIL via native extension): python time reduced by ~12% absolute (from 18% -> 6% of samples), overall p99 small -> 130ms.

Observations / inferred root causes:
- Tokenization remains a meaningful contributor, but not the only one: combined overhead of JSON/header parse + Python shim + scheduler/wakeup dominates on short requests. When tokenizer SIMD is enabled, other components surface as next bottlenecks.
- Frequent short-lived tasks cause heavy park/unpark cycles across cores; context-switch and wakeup costs are additive and show up disproportionately at p99.
- Python per-request startup cost (argument unpack, small validation) is non-trivial for tiny requests; e.g., 2–4 function calls and object allocations per request add up under contention because of GIL acquisition delays.
- Thread affinity reduces cross-core overhead but can harm long-request throughput due to reduced ability to pack heavy work on hot cores. This implies we need an adaptive strategy rather than static affinity.

Microbench snippets (informal):
- Tokenizer micro: input=average-chat-32; simd path: 1400ns/op, fallback: 2700ns/op. For 8B tokens/s target, simd saves ~8 cores across fleet in this mix.
- Header parse micro: json-load naive 2.2us/op, tiny pre-sieve (fast-scan for '{"model') 0.6us/op.

Low-risk mitigations to try (ranked):
1) Add a fast pre-sieve for headers (byte-scan for first non-whitespace + small fixed-pattern match) in Rust before any Python allocation. Minimal surface area, big p95 improvements in sim. Owner: Priya. ETA: 2w pilot.
2) SIMD tokenizer for variable-length mode with threshold heuristic (switch to SIMD only for payloads > 48B to avoid branch mispredict penalty). Owner: Diego. ETA: 3w testing across instance types.
3) Adaptive parking policy: instead of immediate park/unpark, allow a brief cooperative yield (sched_yield or user-space backoff) for tasks < X ms expected. Implement in threadpool: backoff counters escalate to park after N yields. Owner: Evan. ETA: 4w prototype.
4) Move 2 simple hot-path operations out of Python into a minimal C/Rust extension: header-sieve + metric-tag-extract. Owner: Priya + Diego. ETA: 5w.
5) Queue aging + small-request prioritization in scheduler: small requests get an accelerated queue; ensure aging prevents starvation for long requests. Owner: Product/Runtime team. ETA: design 1 week.

Risks / tradeoffs:
- Aggressive prioritization of small requests could decrease throughput for heavy batch users (our large request customers). Need SLIs per-customer to ensure fairness.
- SIMD path complexity: more code paths mean more maintenance and potential regressions on unusual encodings. Must add coverage for surrogate pairs/rare unicode.
- Cooperative yields are sensitive to noisy neighbors and vCPU oversubscription; need knobs per deployment class (hosted vs dedicated).

A/B rollout plan (proposed):
- Canary lane: enable header-sieve + small-request prioritization on 5% of multi-tenant hosts (non-dedicated). Duration: 2 weeks, collect p50/p95/p99 per-request-size band, CPU tokens/s, syscall/wakeup delta.
- Rollout metric gates: p99 small improves >= 15% without p99 large regressing > 3% and no CPU cost > 7% increase.
- If gates pass, enable SIMD tokenizer threshold and adaptive parking together in 10% hosts, then 33% etc.

Instrumentation additions we should add before rollout:
- per-request breakdowns exported (tokenizer_ns, parse_ns, py_handler_ns, scheduler_wait_ns) as tags in existing tracing spans.
- wakeup/futex counts per-thread exported to infra metrics (scrape via eBPF agent).
- add short-lived request sampler that captures backtraces for p99 events for hand analysis.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the exact tipping point for SIMD mispredict overhead vs benefit across instance types (AMD vs Intel vs Graviton)? Need dedicated CPU microbench matrix.
- Are there specific tenant patterns that cause pathological park/unpark (e.g., lots of small synchronous requests vs async) — collect tenant-level samples.
- Does our Python distribution and GC configuration matter significantly for these microbursts (e.g., generational GC causing stop-the-world pauses)? Run controlled tests with GC tuning.

Action items (concrete):
- Priya: implement header-sieve Rust extension + unit tests. (due 2026-03-01)
- Diego: produce SIMD tokenizer threshold PR with cross-platform microbench results. (due 2026-03-08)
- Evan: prototype cooperative-yield threadpool behavior and a microbench harness. (due 2026-03-15)
- Asha: define A/B metric dashboard and write canary run playbook. (due 2026-03-10)

Notes-to-self:
- Keep experiments reproducible: persist loadgen seed, config, and perf data in /mnt/bench-results/<date>/ so we can compare runs.
- Record exact kernel versions for each test (futex semantics drift across linux versions).

If reviewers want, I can extract a one-pager for product with the prioritized mitigations and estimated customer impact (cost/core saved and latency improvement estimates).

-- end of scratchpad --
